subtitle: Practice delegating within your authority: match work with support, explain decision limits, broaden access to development, and respond when the assignment needs to change.
audience: For supervisors and work leads who assign tasks, support development and coordinate decisions within their authorized roles.

lessons.title: Delegation as a leadership duty, not a favor
objectives: Explain delegation as handing over a task together with the authority and support needed to complete it.
Sort your current work into what needs your role, what others could do now and what others could learn to do.
Identify two costs to the team when a leader keeps most of the work.
Describe where your own default about doing work yourself came from and how it affects others.
lessons.teaching:
Delegation is part of the job of leading, not a favor you do when you are busy. The U.S. Office of Personnel Management's 2015 federal managerial framework describes delegation as empowering employees by assigning tasks and granting the authority that goes with them, then providing resources and timely, objective feedback on the work. This federal framework offers a useful planning approach; it does not establish Minnesota delegation authority. Its definition holds three duties together: the task, the authority and the support. Handing over a task without the other two is not delegation. It asks someone to carry work they cannot fully move.

Start by sorting your own work. Keep decisions that require your assigned role or approval, including personnel decisions and commitments you alone are authorized to make. Consult Human Resources or labor relations when duties or personnel procedures are unclear. Confidential work may be assigned only within authorized access and disclosure rules; confidentiality alone does not mean every task must stay with a supervisor. Much of the rest can be handed over or shared, including recurring tasks you mastered long ago, analysis others could do with some support, and parts of larger projects that would help someone grow. A useful test is to ask what someone could do now, what they could learn to do, and what truly needs you.

Doing it all yourself has costs that are easy to miss. The work slows when everything waits for you. Knowledge about how things get done sits with one person, which leaves the team fragile when you are away. People may lose opportunities to develop skills when they cannot gain experience with more demanding work. Ask yourself where you learned that doing the work yourself is the responsible choice. Many leaders were rewarded early in their careers for being the one who always delivered, and that habit can follow them into a role where it holds others back.

Delegation also shapes who gets seen. When a supervisor holds the visible work and hands out only routine tasks, the team's skills stay hidden from the people who make later decisions. Before you decide what to keep, ask who is affected, whose experience of the work you might be missing and how you would find out. A conversation about each person’s interests and workload can reveal options you had not considered. Then decide, and check after a few weeks whether the change made the work better for the people it touches.
lessons.keyPoint: Delegation hands over a task together with the authority and support to complete it. Keep what truly needs your role, share the rest on purpose, and notice what doing it all yourself costs the team.
lessons.example: Practice case: Marisol supervises a licensing team in disability services. Since her promotion she still reviews every provider renewal file herself before it goes out, because she knows the rules well and mistakes are costly. Files now wait a week for her. Ahmed, a licensing consultant with six years on the team, has asked twice to take on final reviews for simpler renewals. Grace, who joined last year, has said she would like to learn the review process. Marisol has an hour free on Friday. In this practice case, agency procedures allow Marisol to assign final review of the simpler renewals to a qualified consultant.
lessons.question: What should Marisol do with her Friday hour?
choices: Meet with Ahmed and Grace to agree which renewals Ahmed can finalize, what Grace will learn first, and when they will check in.
Use the hour to clear the backlog herself, then return to delegation once the files are current and the team's pressure has eased.
Ask Ahmed to take over all final reviews starting Monday so the files move, and tell him to bring her any questions.
feedback: This matches the task to experience, gives Ahmed real authority for a defined set of files and starts Grace's learning. A planned check-in keeps quality visible.
Clearing urgent files may be necessary, but this response postpones the discussion without addressing the bottleneck. Ahmed and Grace still lack an agreed role and learning plan.

This assigns all final reviews without checking their complexity or agreeing on limits and support. Ahmed’s experience does not establish that every review can be transferred, and Grace’s learning interest remains unaddressed.
lessons.reflection: Which part of your work do you keep because only you can do it, and which part do you keep because it feels safer or faster to do it yourself?
lessons.action: List the recurring tasks you handled over the past two weeks. Identify what requires your role and what someone else could do or learn. Choose one permitted assignment, confirm the person’s workload and support, and agree on a first check-in.

check.question: According to the federal managerial framework in this lesson, what turns handing over a task into delegation?
check.correct: The person also receives the authority to act and the support needed to finish.
wrong: The task is written up with a clear deadline before it is assigned to anyone else.
The task goes to the most experienced person so that the result is reliable.
check.feedback: Delegation holds the task, the authority and the support together. A deadline and an experienced person can help, but without authority and support the person cannot fully move the work.

lessons.title: Matching the task, the person and the authority
objectives: Choose a level of authority for a task based on its risk and the person's experience with similar work.
State the outcome, the limits and the check-in points when you hand over a piece of work.
Distinguish a decision the person can make from one that still needs your approval or another area's.
Adapt how you hand over and follow up so the person can take part fully.
lessons.teaching:
Delegation is not all or nothing. Between doing a task yourself and handing it over completely, there are several useful levels. The person can look into something and report back. They can recommend a course and you decide. They can decide and tell you before acting. They can decide and act, then update you at the next check-in. Or they can own the work fully. Naming the level helps both people check whether they understand who decides. These are planning categories, not permissions to transfer authority that law or agency procedures reserve to another role.

Match the level to the task and to the person's experience with similar work. A task with high risk to people served, a legal deadline or public attention may start at a lower level even for an experienced colleague, with later changes based on demonstrated readiness and the authority available. Familiar work may allow substantial independence, but experience does not remove required approval or separation of duties. Base the choice on what the person has done and what the task demands, not on a general impression of their confidence or polish. Consider whether your impression reflects relevant evidence or familiarity with a style like your own.

Be clear about the outcome, the limits and the check-ins when you hand work over. The outcome is what done looks like and who it serves. The limits: the budget, policy and timelines that apply, who else must approve, and anything that must not change. The check-ins: when you will talk, in what form, and what should prompt an earlier conversation. If an assignment would have someone perform substantially all the duties of a temporarily unoccupied position in a different classification, talk with Human Resources first. Minnesota Management and Budget's procedure on work out of class assignments sets rules for those arrangements, and the applicable collective bargaining agreement or compensation plan governs relevant terms. Taking on some different duties does not by itself make an assignment work out of class.

Ask how the person works best, and adapt the handover to fit. Some people want the brief in writing so they can return to it, some prefer to talk it through, and some need materials in an accessible format or captioned meetings. Ask rather than assume what someone needs. Recognize possible accommodation requests even when a person does not use that term. Follow the agency process and promptly forward the request to the appropriate decision maker if you do not hold that role. After the first check-in, ask what was unclear and change how you brief the next piece of work.
lessons.keyPoint: Agree on the outcome, decision limits and check-ins before work begins. Match independence to risk and experience within the authority that agency rules allow.
lessons.example: Practice case: Tomasz, a policy lead in an economic assistance area, asks Jalen, an analyst, to prepare options for changing a county reporting form. Jalen has done similar analysis but has never presented to county partners. Tomasz says only, "Take the lead on this." Two weeks later Jalen shares a recommended form with Rosa, a county partner, who assumes it is final. Tomasz had expected to review options first. Rosa's team has started planning around the new form.
lessons.question: What should Tomasz do now?
choices: Email Rosa that the form is not final, then tell Jalen he will handle all county conversations from here so there is no more confusion.
Let the form stand, since Jalen acted in good faith and reversing it would embarrass him, and plan to be clearer next time.
Own the unclear handover with Jalen, agree on a level for the rest of the work, and contact Rosa together about what is still open.
feedback: Correcting the record matters. Taking every county conversation back, however, does not address the unclear assignment or consider how Jalen could continue within an agreed role.
This spares a hard moment, but it commits the area to a form no one decided on, and Rosa's team keeps planning around a choice that may still change.
This acknowledges the unclear assignment and establishes authority for the remaining work. Contacting Rosa together can correct the misunderstanding while preserving Jalen’s role in the relationship.
lessons.reflection: Think of the last time you asked someone to take the lead on something. How much authority did you mean, and how would they have known?
lessons.action: Before you next hand over a piece of work, write three lines: what done looks like, the limits that apply and when you will check in. Add the level of authority in plain words and share it with the person.

check.question: An authorized delegation can be adjusted within agency rules. The task carries a legal deadline and the colleague is experienced. What does this lesson suggest about the level of authority?
check.correct: Start at a level that fits the risk, then raise it as the work goes well.
wrong: Give full ownership at once, since experience matters more than the task's risk.
Keep the task yourself, since high-risk work should not be delegated to others.
check.feedback: Risk, demonstrated experience and permitted authority all matter. More independence may become appropriate as the work progresses, but it cannot override a required approval or a role-specific duty.

lessons.title: Delegation as development: offering stretch work
objectives: Plan a stretch assignment that names the skill it builds, the criteria for taking it on and the support that comes with it.
Compare how a habit of giving work to whoever is ready looks at different points on the intercultural continuum.
Explain how readiness for stretch work can reflect who received earlier chances.
Draft an offer of delegated work that names its starting level of authority and lets people respond in more than one way.
lessons.teaching:
Delegated work is one of the main ways people grow on the job. The U.S. Office of Personnel Management's 2015 report on learning for leaders describes a developmental assignment as one designed to stretch a person beyond their existing skills. The Center for Creative Leadership's research on how managers and executives learn found challenging assignments to be a main source of growth; its 70-20-10 guideline is a rule of thumb, not a measured law. OPM's managerial framework adds that tasks should be delegated on objective criteria such as skill, experience, developmental needs and interests, workload and fairness.

Ask yourself who usually gets your stretch work, and who has never been offered it. Then ask why those people come to mind first. Examine the actual pattern rather than assuming anyone’s intent. If assignments repeatedly go to the person who asks first or has done similar work, those choices may build an experience advantage. Consider whether other people have had a reasonable opportunity to express interest and prepare.

The intercultural development continuum described by IDI, LLC can help you examine how you offer stretch work, through program-created examples, not by assessing or labeling colleagues. These examples illustrate the orientations; a single choice does not establish anyone’s place on the continuum. A Minimization habit sounds fair: I give stretch work to whoever is ready, and I treat everyone the same. An Acceptance habit notices that readiness often reflects who got earlier chances, and that people show interest differently, some by asking directly and some by waiting to be invited. An Adaptation habit changes the practice: describing the work openly, naming criteria, offering support that helps someone without the earlier chance attempt the work, and asking people who have not raised their hands.

Make the offer specific: the work, the skill it builds, what it takes and the support that comes with it. Support might mean regular check-ins, a more experienced colleague to consult or time freed from other duties. Name the starting level of authority and what would let it grow, so the person knows what they will actually decide. Let people respond in writing or in conversation. Use the agency’s selection requirements and operational needs when making the assignment. Open invitations and appropriate support can broaden access; they do not guarantee selection or replace required qualifications.
lessons.keyPoint: Readiness for stretch work is often built by earlier chances. Offer delegated work openly, with clear criteria and real support, so that development reaches people who have not been offered it before.
lessons.example: Practice case: Priya supervises a waiver program team in disability services that supports lead agencies. A new training series for lead agency staff needs someone to design and deliver it. Kwame has led the last three trainings and is eager to lead again. Nora, a program consultant who knows the policy deeply, has never been asked to train and has not volunteered. Luis, hired eight months ago, said in a recent one-to-one that he wants presenting experience.
lessons.question: How should Priya decide who leads the training series?
choices: Give it to Kwame, who has shown he can do it well, and ask him to include Nora and Luis as helpers on one session each.
Describe the work and its support to the whole team, invite interest in writing or in person, and consider a shared lead with coaching.
Assign it to Nora because she has never had the chance, and tell the team it is her turn so that the decision feels fair to everyone involved.
feedback: This offers some exposure, but Kwame retains the lead role without a fresh review of the criteria, interests or available support. Reliable past work is relevant, but it need not be the only consideration.
This makes the offer visible, lets people respond in a way that suits them and builds in support, so the choice rests on interest, criteria and development.
This corrects the pattern with good intent, but it decides for Nora without asking about her interest, and calling it her turn makes development sound like a rotation.
lessons.reflection: When you hand out work that would help someone grow, what usually makes a person come to mind first, and how might others show interest in ways you miss?
lessons.action: Choose one upcoming piece of work that could stretch someone. Write two sentences on the skill it builds, the support that comes with it and the starting level of authority, and share them with your whole team before you decide who takes it.

check.question: In this course’s illustrative continuum examples, which response reflects an Adaptation habit in offering stretch work?
check.correct: Changing how the work is offered and supported so more people can take it on.
wrong: Giving the work to whoever shows readiness first, so everyone is treated alike.
Noticing that readiness can reflect earlier chances, then choosing the usual person.
check.feedback: In this example, Adaptation means changing the offer and support in response to differences. Recognizing unequal access is useful, but the response must also address the practice. These examples do not assess a person’s developmental orientation.

lessons.title: Supporting and following up without taking it back
objectives: Use questions to understand a routine problem before deciding what advice, support or intervention is needed.
Decide when taking work back is warranted and how to say so openly.
Give specific credit for delegated work in the places where decisions are made.
Plan a short review with the person of what worked, what to change and what to stop.
lessons.teaching:
The hardest moment in delegation comes when the work gets difficult. A leader who knows how to fix the problem is tempted to step in, and stepping in can feel like support. OPM's 2015 managerial framework describes a different skill: asking questions and continuing to ask them while resisting the impulse to give advice for every situation, grounding observations in behavior and facts, and following up periodically. OPM's 2018 memo on coaching adds a boundary. Coaching serves learning and development and does not replace a supervisor's performance management duties, so supervisors must also use applicable agency performance procedures and seek Human Resources guidance when needed. A coaching conversation does not suspend a deadline, reporting duty or required action.

When there is time to explore a routine problem safely, ask questions before taking over. Ask what the person has tried, what options they see and what would help. Share what you have noticed in specific terms, and consider whether a resource, contact or direct explanation would help. Questions are useful, but withholding necessary information does not support learning. FEMA's leadership course advises keeping in contact without hovering, since people learn by doing, while you continue to carry the responsibilities assigned to your role. Deloitte research by Bernadette Dillon and Juliet Bourke describes empowerment as room to handle difficult situations and decide about one's own work. Reassign work when warranted by risk, workload, changing priorities or other legitimate operational needs. Explain the reason and the remaining responsibilities, and involve the person where appropriate. Urgent protective action need not wait for a coaching conversation.

Credit is part of the handover. When delegated work goes well, name the person's contribution where it counts: in updates to leadership, in meetings with partners and in the project's own records. Be specific about what they did. Washington State’s published leadership competencies include everyday recognition as part of developing people. This is a useful example from another state, not a Minnesota requirement. Ask how each person prefers to be recognized, since some would rather have a quiet word than public thanks.

Close the loop with a short review together. Ask what worked, what was harder than expected, what support helped and what was missing. Share your own part, such as where your brief was unclear or a check-in came too late. Then agree on what you will both keep, change or stop, and whether the next piece of work can carry more authority. Periodically review who receives development opportunities and what support is available. Keep personal learning reflections free of unnecessary identifying details, while maintaining authorized assignment and personnel records under agency procedures.
lessons.keyPoint: When delegated work gets difficult, assess the risk and support needed. Explain any reassignment, give appropriate credit, and review together what to keep, change or stop.
lessons.example: Practice case: Ben supervises an eligibility policy team. He asked Dev, an experienced program consultant who has run partner meetings for years, to plan a public input session on a rule change. Ten days before the session, Dev tells Ben the venue fell through and two community groups have raised concerns about the agenda. Ben ran sessions like this for years and knows a venue contact. Dev sounds stretched but has not asked Ben to take over.
lessons.question: What should Ben do in his next conversation with Dev?
choices: Ask what Dev has tried and what would help, offer the venue contact, and agree on an earlier check-in before the session date.
Take over the venue and the agenda himself since time is short, and let Dev run the session logistics on the day itself.
Reassure Dev that he trusts him completely, then step back so that Dev can solve it on his own and grow from the whole experience.
feedback: This keeps Dev in charge, adds the help that matters most right now and brings the next check-in forward. Ben supports the work without taking it back.

Reassigning work may be necessary, but this response does not first establish what Dev has tried or what support could resolve the difficulty. Ben can assess urgency and offer help without automatically taking over both responsibilities.
Trust matters, but stepping back when someone is stretched leaves them alone with the risk. Support and a closer check-in show trust better than distance does.
lessons.reflection: When someone you hand work to starts to struggle, what do you feel pulled to do, and what would help you ask one more question first?
lessons.action: This week, hold a short review with someone you handed work to: what worked, what was hard and what support helped. Agree on one thing to keep, one to change and the authority for the next piece, and ask yourself who has not yet been offered work like it.

check.question: For a routine problem with time to explore options safely, someone you delegated to needs help. What does this lesson suggest you do first?
check.correct: Ask what they have tried and what would help before offering your own answer.
wrong: Solve it quickly yourself, then explain how you did it so they learn the method.
Leave them to work it out alone, since stepping in would undercut their authority.
check.feedback: Questions help you understand what has been tried and what support is needed. Direct advice or intervention may also be appropriate; the point is to avoid taking over automatically when supported problem-solving is possible.

cards.back: Assigning work with appropriate authority and support. The person carries the assigned responsibilities, while you retain those attached to your role.
The decisions a person may make within an assignment. State required approvals clearly; experience and successful work do not override limits imposed by policy or law.
An agreed time and format for talking about delegated work, plus the signs that should prompt an earlier talk, so neither person is left guessing.
Work designed to stretch someone beyond their current skills so they can meet more complex demands. It needs clear criteria and real support to be fair.
Reassigning work for a legitimate operational reason. Explain the change, clarify responsibilities and involve the person where appropriate; act promptly when risk requires it.

aid.heading: Before you hand it over
items: Sort the task: needs my role, someone could do now, or someone could learn.
Ask who has not yet been offered work like this, and why.
Confirm what authority can be delegated, then choose a level that fits the task’s risk and the person’s relevant experience.
If the work would shift someone into another classification's duties, talk with Human Resources first.

aid.heading: When you hand it over
items: Say what done looks like and who the work serves.
Name the limits: budget, policy, timelines and who else must approve.
State the authority in plain words: report back, recommend, decide and tell me first, decide and update me, or own it fully.
Agree on check-in times, a format that works for the person and what should prompt an earlier call.
Name the support that comes with the work.

aid.heading: While it is underway and after
items: Stay in touch without hovering. For routine problems, ask what has been tried and what support is needed; act promptly when risk requires it.
Explain any reassignment and the remaining responsibilities. Involve the person where appropriate, without delaying urgent action.
Give specific credit in appropriate updates and records, and consider the person’s preference before public recognition.
Review together what to keep, change or stop, and whether the next piece can carry more authority.

sources.title: U.S. Office of Personnel Management — Federal Supervisory and Managerial Frameworks and Guidance (September 2015)
sources.note: Adapted from the definition of delegation (tasks, authority, resources and feedback), the objective criteria for delegating, and the coaching objectives on questions before advice. Federal guidance from 2015.

sources.title: U.S. Office of Personnel Management — Effective Learning Interventions for Developing ECQs (November 2015)
sources.note: Supports the description of a developmental assignment as work designed to stretch a person beyond existing skills. A 2015 federal literature review built on OPM's earlier leadership competency model.

sources.title: U.S. Office of Personnel Management — Coaching in the Federal Government (memorandum, September 10, 2018)
sources.note: Supports the point that coaching is for learning and development and does not replace a supervisor's performance management duties. Federal guidance; state rules come from Minnesota sources.

sources.title: Washington State Department of Enterprise Services — Enterprise Leadership Competencies (version 3, 2021)
sources.note: The indexed publisher document supports everyday appreciation and recognition under Develops People. Cited as another state’s example, not a Minnesota requirement.

sources.title: Deloitte University Press — Bernadette Dillon and Juliet Bourke, The six signature traits of inclusive leadership (2016)
sources.note: Supports the description of empowerment as room to handle difficult situations and make decisions about one's own work. Consulting research from 2016, not peer reviewed.

sources.title: IDI, LLC — The Intercultural Development Continuum (IDC)
sources.note: Supports the names and descriptions of the continuum orientations. The stretch-work examples are this program’s illustrations, not validated assessments or descriptions supplied by the publisher.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Administrative Procedure 17.1, Work Out of Class Assignments (revised 2024)
sources.note: Defines work out of class for permanent or probationary classified employees performing substantially all duties of a temporarily unoccupied position in another classification. Some different duties alone do not qualify. Applicable collective bargaining agreements or compensation plans govern relevant terms; consult Human Resources.

sources.title: FEMA Emergency Management Institute — IS-240.B Leadership and Influence, Instructor Guide (February 2014)
sources.note: Lesson 6.10 supports appropriate authority, monitoring without hovering and acknowledgement of contributions. Historical federal training used as guidance; completing this program does not establish completion of a FEMA course.

sources.title: Center for Creative Leadership — The 70-20-10 Rule for Leadership Development (2025)
sources.note: CCL’s 2025 practitioner article describes challenging assignments and experience-based leader development. The course uses the framework as a planning guideline, not a prescribed allocation of each employee’s learning time.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — HR/LR Policy 1433, ADA Reasonable Accommodation
sources.note: Supports recognizing requests without special wording and promptly forwarding them to the appropriate decision maker under agency procedures.
